title: The fear of the LORD
lead: The fear of the LORD is the Bible's name for the right response to God: awe, reverence and obedience together. Wisdom books call it the start of wisdom, the Law ties it to keeping God's commands, and Ecclesiastes ends with it as the whole of being human.

sections.h: The fear of the LORD across the Bible
sections.b: The Hebrew yir'ah, "fear", covers both terror and reverence, and when its object is God it means a life ordered by awe of him. Abraham is shown to "fear God" when he does not hold back his son (Genesis 22:12), and the Hebrew midwives "feared God" and would not obey Pharaoh (Exodus 1:17). The Law joins fear to love and service: "to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him" (Deuteronomy 10:12). The wisdom books make it the foundation of wisdom: "The fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins" (Proverbs 1:7; compare Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10), and Job's poem on wisdom ends, "the fear of the Lord is wisdom" (Job 28:28). Isaiah's promised ruler from the line of Jesse has "a spirit to know and to fear the LORD" (Isaiah 11:2). The New Testament keeps the language: the early church lived "in the fear of the Lord" (Acts 9:31).
sections.refs: Genesis 22:12; Exodus 1:17; Deuteronomy 10:12; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 9:10; Psalm 111:10; Job 28:28; Isaiah 11:2–3; Acts 9:31

sections.b: Readers have long asked how fear of God fits with love for him. Jewish teachers distinguished fear of punishment from the higher fear of reverence before God's greatness, and Christian writers set 1 John 4:18 ("perfect love throws fear out") beside the Psalms' call to serve the LORD with fear (Psalm 2:11). Most read the biblical phrase as reverent awe that includes love and trust, not dread alone.
